articles.title: GV300 Showcase
articles.contents:
Introduction
This work demonstrates some of the code I have created during my final year
Advanced Quantitative Political Analysis module.
Code chunk


library(tidyverse)

uk_csv <- "https://electionresults.parliament.uk/general-elections/6/candidacies.csv"
uk_raw <- readr::read_csv(uk_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)

names(uk_raw) <- names(uk_raw) %>% tolower() %>% str_replace_all("\\s+", "_")

uk1 <- uk_raw %>%
  filter(!`election_is_by-election`)

uk2 <- uk1 %>%
  select(
    constituency = constituency_name,
    country      = country_name,
    valid_votes  = candidate_vote_count,
    electorate   = electorate
  )

uk3 <- uk2 %>%
  group_by(country, constituency) %>%
  summarise(
    valid_votes = sum(valid_votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    electorate  = max(electorate, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

uk <- uk3 %>%
  mutate(turnout_registered = 100 * valid_votes / electorate) %>%
  filter(is.finite(turnout_registered), electorate > 0)

non_voter_analysis <- uk %>%
  mutate(non_voters = electorate - valid_votes)

total_non_voters <- sum(non_voter_analysis$non_voters)
total_electorate <- sum(non_voter_analysis$electorate)
total_voters <- sum(non_voter_analysis$valid_votes)
non_voter_percentage <- 100 * total_non_voters / total_electorate

top_non_voters <- non_voter_analysis %>%
  arrange(desc(non_voters)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  select(constituency, country, electorate, valid_votes, 
         non_voters, turnout_registered)

top_non_voters

 1 Birmingham Ladywood       England      83693       36579      47114

 3 Leeds South               England      75953       31678      44275
 4 Wolverhampton South East  England      77473       33382      44091
 5 Salford                   England      83633       39704      43929

Visualisation


library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
library(here)
kidiq <- read_csv(here::here("_data", "kidiq-2.csv"))

kidiq <- kidiq %>%
  mutate(
    ability_level = case_when(
      mom_iq <= quantile(mom_iq, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Low ability",
      mom_iq <= quantile(mom_iq, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Medium ability",
      TRUE ~ "High ability"
    ),
     outcome_level = case_when(
      kid_score <= quantile(kid_score, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Low outcome",
      kid_score <= quantile(kid_score, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Medium outcome",
      TRUE ~ "High outcome"
    ),
    iq_group = case_when(
      mom_iq <= quantile(mom_iq, 0.33, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Lower IQ",
      mom_iq <= quantile(mom_iq, 0.67, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Middle IQ",
      TRUE ~ "Higher IQ"
    ),
    surprising_case = case_when(
      ability_level == "High ability" & outcome_level == "Low outcome" ~ "High ability, low outcome",
      ability_level == "Low ability" & outcome_level == "High outcome" ~ "Low ability, high outcome",
      TRUE ~ "Expected pattern"
    ),
        family_advantage = case_when(
      mom_hs == 0 & mom_work <= 2 ~ "Low advantage",
      mom_hs == 0 & mom_work > 2 ~ "Mixed advantage",
      mom_hs == 1 & mom_work <= 2 ~ "Mixed advantage", 
      mom_hs == 1 & mom_work > 2 ~ "High advantage"
    ),
    mom_round_iq = round(kidiq $ mom_iq, digits = 0)
  )

# this reorders levels of advantage to a logical order of low, mixed, and high.
kidiq $ family_advantage <- factor(kidiq $ family_advantage, levels = c("Low advantage", "Mixed advantage",
                                                                        "High advantage"))

# this reorders levels of mom IQ to a logical order of lower, middle, and high.
kidiq $ iq_group <- factor(kidiq $ iq_group, levels = c("Lower IQ", "Middle IQ", "Higher IQ"))
                  
 kidiq %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mom_round_iq, y = kid_score, color = surprising_case)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(data = subset(kidiq, surprising_case == "Expected pattern"),
              aes(x = mom_round_iq, y = kid_score),
              method = 'lm', color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ family_advantage) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Expected pattern" = "gray", 
                               "High ability, low outcome" = "lightgreen", 
                               "Low ability, high outcome" = "#F781BF"), name = "Surprising Cases") +
  labs(
    title = "The Relationship Between Children's Test Scores and Mother's IQs
and the Impact of Familial Advantage",
    subtitle = "Children with low familial advantage have a stronger positive relationship between 
mother's IQ and test results than mixed and high advantage groups. This suggests
childrens' outcomes are not purely based on merit.", 
    x = "Mother's IQ (proxy for 'ability')",
    y = "Child's Test Score",
    caption = "Data: Children's test scores and mother's characteristics"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank()) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())



What the code does and what the figure shows.
After loading the data set, the first chunk of code creates meaningful categories,
identifying: the level of the mother’s ability, the outcome level of children’s
scores, groups the mothers by iq, identifies outliers, filters the mother’s by
levels of advantage, and finally rounded the mother’s IQs. The following two lines
of code reorder family advantage and mom IQ to make the visualisation follow
a logical order (from low to high). The visualisation code displays the children’s
test scores as points, whilst adding a regression line on top to show how the
relationship between test scores and IQ vary across backgrounds. Surprising cases
are coloured differently.
The figure shows that there is a positive relationship between mother’s IQ and
child’s test score across all backgrounds. This means that children of mothers with
higher IQ scores are more likely to test highly. This relationship is strongest
in those with low familial advantage. The other two groups have more surprising
cases (when the predicted relationship is not found) than low familial advantage
but this may be due to them having larger sample sizes.
Link to repository
https://github.com/martha-png/GV300-Assignment

articles.title: GV300 Showcase
articles.contents:
Introduction
This work demonstrates some of the work I have undertaken as part of my
undergraduate studies. It explores the use of quantitative methods on text,
i.e. text analysis.
The first section investigates elements of textual data, specifically whether
UK political party manifestos are getting shorter or longer. The first graph
shows that over time, party manifestos have lengthened, demonstrated via the
rise in the number of sentences found in each manifesto. The second graph seeks
to understand this relationship further by splitting the data by party to
understand if this trend is observed across all parties. It finds that it is.
The second section conducts a simple Naive Bayes classifier which is a statistical
classification technique that can be used for text classification. In this case
it classifies text into Republican or Democrat. The classifier is found to
perform poorly in this context.
The rise in the number of sentences in political manifestos
Calculating sentence numbers


library(readtext)
library(quanteda)
library(ggplot2)

manifestos <- readtext("UK Manifestos/*.txt", docvarsfrom = c("filenames"))

manifestos_corpus <- corpus(manifestos, docnames = manifestos$doc_id)

num_sentences <- nsentence(manifestos_corpus)
head(num_sentences)

Con1918.txt Con1922.txt Con1923.txt Con1924.txt Con1929.txt 
         56          42          59          85         222 
Con1931.txt 
         30 

This section loads the data, turns the text files into a ‘corpus’ and shows how
many sentences are in each manifesto.
Sorting dates


nms <- names (manifestos_corpus)

dates <- as.numeric(gsub('[^[:digit:]]','', nms))
head(dates)

[1] 1918 1922 1923 1924 1929 1931

This has created new objects for the names of the text files and the dates
each manifesto was published in.
Plotting the number of sentences by year


sentence_df <- data.frame(num_sentences, dates)

sentence_df$doc_id <- manifestos$doc_id

sentence_df$party <- substr(sentence_df$doc_id, 1, 3)
  
ggplot(sentence_df, aes(x = dates, y = num_sentences))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(
  x = "Year",
  y = "Number of Sentences") +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black",size = 1, fill = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"))



A new data frame was created for the graph. ‘doc_id’ is added to the data frame
for the next graph that explores whether all parties see an increase in
manifesto length. The separate parties are also identified.
The graph shows that there has been a rise in the number of sentences in
manifestos.
Plotting the number of sentences by party


ggplot(sentence_df, aes(x = dates, y = num_sentences))+
  geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~party)+
  labs(
  x = "Year",
  y = "Number of Sentences") +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black",size = 1, fill = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"))



This second graph shows that the growth of manifest length is consistent across
all parties.
Naive Bayes Classification
Developing a detailed data set


library(stringr)
library(quanteda.textmodels)
library(lattice)
library(caret)

speeches <- readtext("Concession Speeches/*.txt") 

speeches_corpus <- corpus(speeches)

nam <-names(speeches_corpus)

speeches_corpus$Dates  <- paste(as.numeric(gsub('[^[:digit:]]','',
                                                names(speeches_corpus))))

speeches_corpus$Party <- str_sub(nam, start= -5, -5)

speeches_corpus$PNames <- str_sub(nam, end = -12)

summary(speeches_corpus)

This firstly loads the data and creates a ‘corpus’. It collects the names, dates,
parties, and president names. The summary shows the new columns which provides
useable data for analysis and classification.
Creating paragraphs


speeches_paragraph <- corpus_reshape(speeches_corpus, to = "paragraphs", 
                                     use_docvars = TRUE)

table(speeches_paragraph$Party)


  D   R 
157 180 

To increase the data available, the speeches are split into paragraphs. I check
the data to see if the balance of political parties is equal because an imbalance
will see the classifier over predict. In this case, there is an imbalance with
more Republicans than Democrats.
Data cleaning


speech_tokens <- tokens(speeches_paragraph, remove_punct = TRUE,
                        remove_symbols = TRUE, split_hyphens = TRUE,
                        remove_numbers = TRUE)

speeches_clean <- tokens_wordstem(speech_tokens)

speeches_clean <- tokens_remove(speeches_clean,
                                pattern = c("applpaus", "applause"))

speeches_clean <- tokens_select(speeches_clean, c("*st", "*th", "*rd"),
                                selection = "remove")

speeches_clean <- dfm(speeches_clean)

speeches_clean <- dfm_remove(speeches_clean,
                      stopwords("english"))

speeches_clean <- speeches_clean[, order(featnames(speeches_clean))]


The first line of code provides a list of words from the speeches. Then the
ending of words are removed, spelling mistakes are removed, and special endings
such as the ‘st’ in ‘1st’ are removed. Then a data frame matrix is made which
provides a better structure for analysis. Filler words such as ‘and’ and ‘the’
are removed and the remaining words are ordered alphabetically.
Training the system


Concession_dfm_train <- speeches_clean[1:268, ]

Concession_dfm_test <- speeches_clean[269:337, ]

Concession_train_labels <- speeches_paragraph$Party[1:268]

Concession_test_labels <- speeches_paragraph$Party[269:337]

Concession_dfm_train

This chunk trains the system using an 80/20 split, meaning that the model is
trained on 80% of the data and the remaining 20% is used to evaluate its
performance.
Applying the text model


nb_model <- textmodel_nb(Concession_dfm_train, docvars(Concession_dfm_train,
                                                       "Party"))
summary(nb_model)

The model assumes that all words are independent from one another (doesn’t
consider how they function in a sentence) and that their position doesn’t matter.
To understand if the results are accurate further evaluation is needed.
Removing words not included in the training vocabulary


dfmat_matched <- dfm_match(Concession_dfm_test, features =
                             featnames(Concession_dfm_train))
                           
actual_class <- dfmat_matched$Party

predicted_class <- predict(nb_model, newdata = dfmat_matched)


Because some words in the test data were not included in the training data they
are removed and no probability is included in the model.
Checking if the system works


tab_class <- table(predicted_class, actual_class)

cfm <- confusionMatrix(tab_class, mode="everything")

This feedback shows that the accuracy of the system is 59%. The recall of 0.83
shows that if finds most of the Democrat cases however, with a precision of 0.2,
it is usually wrong. Ultimately, the model is unreliable.
